segments.narration: Empty frames have hung in this Boston museum since 1990. Thirteen of them. The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum refuses to take them down.
March eighteenth, 1990. Two men in police uniforms rang the side door at 1:24 a.m. The guard buzzed them in.
Eighty-one minutes inside. They cut a Vermeer and two Rembrandts out of their frames and left with thirteen works worth half a billion dollars.
So why has nobody been arrested? The statute of limitations ran out in 1995. By 2015 the FBI said both thieves were already dead.
Isabella Gardner's will froze her collection exactly as she left it. So the frames stay empty, and a ten-million-dollar reward stays unclaimed.

verdicts.claim: On 18 March 1990 two men dressed as police officers were buzzed into the museum at about 1:24 a.m. by a guard.
verdicts.note: Thieves admitted 1:24 a.m., guard Rick Abath saw apparent police uniforms on CCTV and opened the side entrance.

verdicts.claim: Thirteen works including a Vermeer and two Rembrandts were taken in an 81-minute robbery, later valued by the FBI at about 500 million dollars.
verdicts.note: 13 works; The Concert (Vermeer), The Storm on the Sea of Galilee and A Lady and Gentleman in Black (Rembrandt); robbery lasted 81 minutes; FBI valuation raised to 500 million by 2000. Narration says 'cut out of their frames', which matches the recorded damage to the canvases.

verdicts.claim: The statute of limitations on the theft expired in 1995, and in 2015 the FBI said both thieves were dead.
verdicts.note: Limitations expired in 1995, so prosecution for the theft is barred; FBI stated in 2015 that both thieves had died, without naming them.

verdicts.claim: Isabella Stewart Gardner's will requires that her collection's arrangement never be altered, and the museum offers a 10 million dollar reward.
